source.title: MLP Memory: A Retriever-Pretrained Memory for Large Language Models
source.authors: Ru-Bin Wei; Jia-Qi Cao; Jia-Rui Wang; Ju-Shi Kai; Qi-Peng Guo; Bo-Wen Zhou; Zhou-Han Lin

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures test perplexity across model-size and training-compute sweeps and fits power laws, using the same general scaling measurement as the claim, but on GPT-2 and an augmented architecture in its own settings.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-perplexity scaling results in Section 5.1 and Appendix J. QA, general NLP, hallucination, distribution, and efficiency results do not measure the scaling versions here. The reported choices of loss weight, input layer, interpolation weight, and k are not scaling outcomes and are not rows. Previously published scaling results cited in the paper are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits Kaplan-form power laws, PPL = (βN)^γ, to test perplexity over GPT-2 sizes from 124M to 1.5B. It does this for continued-trained decoder-only GPT-2 and for GPT-2 + MLP Memory, on WikiText-103 (~100M tokens) and a mixed Web set (~600M tokens). That is a direct, if narrow, result on V1 and on the data-dependence of exponents (V7). The setting is new: small continued-training corpora and a memory-augmented architecture. The fits are mainly used to argue the method scales better, but the decoder-only baseline fits are reported in their own right.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors claim exponent improvements of 17.5% (WikiText-103) and 24.1% (Web) over decoder-only GPT-2. They also claim continued gains with more training compute at GPT2-xl scale without overfitting. Separately, they conclude that larger memory gives diminishing returns, with smaller memory the best performance-efficiency trade-off (Appendix J).
record.recipe_differences: Uses power-law fits to test perplexity while sweeping model size and compute, but tests GPT-2 and an externally augmented MLP Memory architecture on WikiText-103 and a mixed Web dataset rather than reproducing the original models and full scaling setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted parameter-scaling exponents vary across the reported architectures and datasets. The compute result is reported for GPT2-xl scale on the Web dataset only.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a retriever-imitating MLP memory steepens the parameter-scaling exponent: 0.143→0.168 on WikiText-103 and 0.216→0.268 on Web.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural augmentation (external parametric memory) changes the scaling exponent itself, not just the offset.

record.problems: Section 5.1 assigns the equations (9.3 · 10^-8 N)^-0.143 and (1.1 · 10^-6 N)^-0.168 to WikiText-103, and (7.7 · 10^-5 N)^-0.216 and (5.0 · 10^-4 N)^-0.268 to the Web dataset. Figure 5 appears to display the latter pair for WikiText-103 and the former pair for Web, so the dataset-to-equation mapping is inconsistent. The parameter sweep spans less than two orders of magnitude, and the compute result is presented in a figure without numerical fit parameters or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: None of the reported parameter- or compute-scaling results were left out.

untested.parts: Token-count and compute scaling with fitted exponents; ranges beyond about one order of magnitude in parameters; training from scratch.
No extrapolation from small fits to larger runs.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities. The repeated-data compute curve (r5) has no fit.
Downstream scores are not related to scale or loss.
Parameter counting, schedule, fitting method, published-law disagreement, curvature.

record.verdict_notes: I changed the tranche from T1 to T3 because this is continued training of pretrained GPT-2 on small corpora with an augmented architecture. The fits use perplexity rather than loss, give no uncertainty, and cover about one order of magnitude. Figure 5 panel equations are swapped relative to the Section 5.1 text; the verdict follows the text. r6 and r7 are unlinked as baseline and method comparisons. r8 and r9 are rebaselined to r7.

versions.untested_parts: The parameter sweep covers GPT-2 sizes from 124M to 1.5B and the compute result is described but not given as a fitted compute power law. The paper does not establish the claim over several orders of magnitude for parameters, tokens, or compute; it does not vary token count as a scaling variable.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token split is reported.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No non-text modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling law is tested.
Downstream benchmark scores are reported, but not their predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

The results show differences in fitted exponents across the tested architectures and datasets, but do not test the effects of parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, fitting methods, compute-optimal allocation, published-law disagreement, or curves bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: GPT-2 decoder-only scaling sweep
rows.operation_detail: Fit test-perplexity power law as model parameter count varies under fixed compute.
rows.note: The body assigns this fit to WikiText-103. Figure 5 appears to associate a different displayed equation with the WikiText-103 panel; see problems.
rows.check: The 'fit' is to perplexity, not log-loss, using 4 points across about one order of magnitude, with no uncertainty. The subject is pretrained GPT-2 continued-trained on WikiText-103, not trained from scratch. The dataset is small enough that data may bottleneck. Figure 5 labels this equation as the Web panel, while the body text assigns it to WikiText-103.

rows.subject: GPT2-xl-scale overall model architecture (GPT-2 + MLP Memory)
rows.stage_stated: additional training on the Web dataset
rows.operation_detail: Measure test perplexity after varying training FLOPs at fixed model size.
rows.note: The text says perplexity becomes significantly lower with increasing training compute and reports no signs of overfitting; no numerical values or fitted compute exponent are given.
rows.check: This is a figure-only result at fixed size (GPT2-xl + MLP Memory). Perplexity falls from roughly 8.0 to 6.9 over about 10–50×10^18 FLOPs, read off the axis. No fit is given, so power-law form cannot be judged. At ~1.5B parameters and a 600M-token dataset, 5×10^19 FLOPs implies several epochs, so this is repeated data.

rows.subject: GPT2-large
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate test perplexity as the number of MLP Memory layers is varied; base-model reference.
rows.note: Reference value for the memory-size comparison; this single point does not establish a power law.
rows.check: A single base-model reference point (GPT2-large, PPL 15.81), not a scaling observation.

rows.subject: GPT2-large + MLP Memory (8 layers, 221M)
rows.operation_detail: Vary MLP Memory capacity by layer count and measure test perplexity.
rows.note: Perplexity is lower than the base reference, but this comparison does not establish a power law.
rows.check: Base versus +memory compares the study's method against its baseline, not a scaling step. It should serve as the baseline for r8 and r9.

rows.subject: GPT2-large + MLP Memory (15 layers, 359M)
rows.operation_detail: Vary MLP Memory capacity by layer count and measure test perplexity.
rows.note: Perplexity is lower than the base reference, but this comparison does not establish a power law.
rows.check: The baseline should be r7 (8-layer, 221M memory, PPL 11.41), not GPT2-large. Going from 221M to 359M memory drops PPL only 11.41→11.35, about 0.5%.

source_check.correct: State for V1: cannot_determine. Table 13 reports GPT2-large PPL 15.81, 8-layer/221M memory PPL 11.41, and 15-layer/359M memory PPL 11.35. The stated base-model baseline is correct; 11.41 is the relevant additional comparator for memory growth.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix I, Table 12; Appendix J, Table 13 and accompanying paragraph, lines 1932–1975.
source_check.problem: A small perplexity improvement from memory growth does not demonstrate an incomplete loss power law; no such law is fitted in this ablation.

rows.subject: GPT2-large + MLP Memory (36 layers, 772M)
rows.operation_detail: Vary MLP Memory capacity by layer count and measure test perplexity.
rows.note: Perplexity is lower than the base reference, but this comparison does not establish a power law.
rows.check: The baseline should be r7. Memory grows 3.5× (221M→772M), which is roughly 1.0B→1.55B total, yet PPL drops only about 1.4% (11.41→11.25). The r2 exponent of 0.168 would predict about 7%. Memory is scaled by depth at fixed width.

source_check.correct: State for V1: cannot_determine. Table 13 reports GPT2-large PPL 15.81, 8-layer/221M memory PPL 11.41, and 36-layer/772M memory PPL 11.25. Memory grows approximately 3.49× and perplexity falls approximately 1.40% relative to the 8-layer configuration. The stated base-model baseline is correct.

relation.reason: Section 5.1 reports original scaling experiments and different fitted exponents across datasets, providing evidence on V7 rather than merely citing or applying an existing law.

tranche.reason: The study reports its own scaling fits in a new setting: continued-trained GPT-2 and retriever-pretrained MLP Memory. Its dataset-dependent perplexity exponents bear on V7, although its fits do not directly test V1's loss functional form.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v4 dated 27 February 2026. Equations (8)–(9) conflict with Figure 5's dataset mapping; fits use perplexity and report no uncertainty. Table 13 explicitly supplies the valid 15.81 base-model baseline; 11.41 is the additional comparator needed to quantify memory growth.

statements.correction: Appendix J, Table 13: fixed GPT2-large backbone; memory 221M→772M, approximately 3.49×; layers 8→36; WikiText-103 PPL 11.41→11.25, approximately 1.40% reduction; diminishing returns from memory growth; no fitted loss power law.
statements.problem: The memory-growth figures are correct, but their use as evidence limiting V1 is unsupported. Appendix J neither fits a loss power law nor establishes a comparable expected scaling curve for memory-only growth.
